title: Are You Praising Too Much To Start The School Year? ool-year/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin warns that the excitement and novelty of the start of a new school year makes teachers especially prone to over-praising students, straying from his usual guideline of reserving praise for exceptional effort or genuinely new, challenging learning. He identifies three specific harms of excessive early-year praise: it lowers the classroom bar right from the start by treating ordinary, expected behavior as special; it devalues true accomplishment by equating everyday routines with hard-won achievements like a well-crafted essay; and it costs teachers respect and attention, since students sense insincerity and eventually tune out even genuine praise. He urges teachers to resist the pressure of a dominant educational culture that says praise can't be overdone, and instead commit to praising only work, effort, or character that genuinely stands out and moves them — delivered honestly, from the heart.
points: The excitement of a new school year makes teachers especially prone to over-praising ordinary, expected behavior.
Praising everyday or expected behavior lowers the classroom's standard of excellence right from the outset.
Excessive praise devalues true accomplishment by equating routine tasks with genuinely hard-won achievements.
Students sense insincere or over-frequent praise, which erodes respect and causes even warranted praise to be tuned out.
Praise should be reserved for effort or achievement that is genuinely new, challenging, or moving — delivered honestly.
quotes: That is, we recommend praise based on exceptional effort or new (but challenging) learning.
So you go overboard. You praise too often. You praise too enthusiastically. You praise for things that, frankly, aren’t worthy of it.
When you stray outside the guidelines of effective, meaningful praise, you send the message that the common, the everyday, and the expected is worthy of special recognition.
When you jump out of your shoes to give praise for what your students have already proven they can do, or for average or expected work, you render praise for true accomplishment less meaningful.
Teachers who praise often, loud, and carelessly struggle with listening and respect because they prove themselves early on to be disingenuous.
Commit yourself to praising only new and challenging learning. Praise effort that goes beyond what your class or an individual student has done before.
